Understanding how Unreal Engine 5 projects are structured is very important as Unreal Engine 5 projects are set up in a slightly different way than you might be used to in traditional applications. This is because in a traditional application, you generally use a single project file to visualize your scene. So when we're inside a Photoshop and we save, we're going to save it to a .psd. Or inside of Word when we save, we're going to save to the .doc or the same for Maya if

we save, we're going to save to the .mb format. Now Unreal has a slightly different approach to this. When you're inside of Unreal Engine 5 and you want to import something such as a model, a texture, audio, or animations, all of that is going to be stored in the content folder and use a .usset file format. There are two other file formats that we should be aware of. The first one is the level file format. This is called the .umap file format.

And this is for any levels that we happen to be saving. And levels is a term for what we place actors or our content and we light and it's what the end user ends up seeing in your project. Now if we are creating, say, a material or editing an asset inside of Unreal, whatever we're doing inside of there is going to be saved again in the .usset file format.

Again, if we are importing something such as a static mesh or maybe a texture, whatever we export will be done is, say, a .fbx or a .png. And when we bring that into Unreal, that's going to be imported and then saved as this .usset file format. Now here is an example of an Unreal Engine project folder. you would need to make that change inside of our UMAP. Now the problem with this is that the UMAP folder was or should say the UMAP file is unique and only one person can have it checked out at one time. This means that whenever I want to make a change to it I either have to wait for somebody else to finish making their changes or come up with a complex way to work on my stuff and then somehow merge it with theirs later on.

This can create a lot of conflicts especially as teams start to grow in size. With Unreal Engine 5 we've introduced a new file system called one file per actor which reduces overlaps between users and does this by saving data for instance the vectors in external files and this actually removes the need to save everything to the UMAP file. So instead of everything being saved to the UMAP file it's now linked to the UMAP file

of the level. just be on the lookout for that.

Understanding a few things about how Unreal deals with content is important as this will ensure that whatever content you're bringing into the engine will function in the way that you want without any unforeseen performance issues. And the first thing we're going to talk about in the content pipeline is the unit of measurement Unreal uses when dealing with static or skeletal meshes. Unit 5 uses centimeters for its unit of measurement. So this means that one Unreal unit equals one centimeter.

It's best to make sure that your digital content creation tools such as 3max, Maya, Blender, or whatever tools you happen to use have their system or scene scale set to centimeters. This way you can avoid any and all scaling issues from your pipeline. The next thing in our content pipeline I'd like to talk about deals with textures. Now textures for the best performance should always be a power of 2 in either the X or

the Y axis. This means that they can range from 2 by 16 to 128 by 256 all the way up to 4096 by 8192. Textures do not have to be square so 64 by 64, 128 by 128 is good but you can also have 128 by 256 or 1024 by 2048. Textures just need to maintain this power of 2 ratio in the X or the Y axis.

Unreal Engine also supports on import a number of uncompressed and compressed formats. So for uncompressed on imports you can bring in BMP, TARGA, and PSD or you can bring in PNG, JPG, DDS, and HDR depending again on what format meets the needs of your project. When importing content into Unreal there's a couple of different ways we can do this. You can either drag and drop right from the OS folder or your desktop right into the content browser or you can click the add button in the content browser and then from there you

You can even download content right from within the fab browser inside of the editor for anything that you have in your library.

I'll go with a total of 3 or maybe 4 clicks for now. You can exit the Scatter command with a right click, but still bring about changes to what you did. For example, all three grass types have been scattered with default options.
You can select one or more and adjust their settings, such as Size, Color Tint, Dryness and more. You can also decide to add another type after the fact, and scatter that one a bit more.

An Eraser tool lets you remove any excess around the boundary areas. I will stop here, but feel free to experiment a bit more with these tools. You can also check out the final file named 06-Final if you want to get a few more ideas. Keep in mind that a few containers have been turned off in the final file to increase performance.

You just need to enable them again to view the full scene. This marks the end of the Twinmotion Part 1 class, the Basics. Once you are comfortable with the tools you learned about here, then you can learn about the next steps in Part 2, where you work with additional tools. You'll learn about man-made lights to create night scenarios, as well as media output to save still images and animation videos to disk, as well as producing a self-executable project that you can share with people who do not have Twinmotion installed.

In this class, you have taken your first steps into Twinmotion, a real-time visualization tool based on Unreal Engine. You've experimented with a typical workflow, first by ingesting data. You then learned to add context on how to embellish the scene with the help of an extensive assets library. You added materials, characters and vehicles among other things, and learned how to create and store your own user library. You also learned how to create and scatter vegetation for a more natural environment.

The next class will teach you other tools in Twinmotion, which will include creating and adjusting man-made lights for night scenes, as well as outputting media to disk in the form of images, panoramas and videos. See you then!

Hello everyone, and welcome to this introductory class on Twinmotion. My name is Amer Yassine, I'm an Unreal Engine and Twinmotion instructor, and I will be your host today. Today we look at Twinmotion. This is in fact part 2 of a 3-part class on Twinmotion. If you are new to Twinmotion and haven't acquired the basics yet, then you may want to first check out the introductory class entitled Twinmotion Part 1, The Basics, before attending this one. In this part 2 class, you learn about additional tools that give you more flexibility, from animation to productivity tools.

You then dig into lighting and see what is on offer, especially with man-made lights to support night scenes. From there, you learn about media output, and how to set up still images, panoramas and videos to export to this. You also learn to export self-executable presentations that you can share with your clients and audience. With that, others can enjoy your work without needing to have Twinmotion installed. Finally, you learn to work in phases, which is capturing an animation of the phases of construction of your project.
And so, if you're ready, let's dive in.

To start off this course, we'll look at a set of Twinmotion tools that are designed to make your work easier. Many of those are the types of tools that you would normally spend time building in real-time engines using code, but here, they are ready to be used right out of the box. To learn about these tools, you need to fire up Twinmotion. I am using Community version 2023.2, which was the latest release version at the time I was recording these videos. You also need to open the project named One Tools that was provided to you.

This project shows the end results of the part 1 portion of this class. First, we'll look at animators. Zoom in on the doors on the main building's second level. You can switch camera speeds using the 1 through 6 hotkeys. The idea is to make these doors open as the camera approaches. In Unreal Engine, you could write a blueprint to that effect if you know how to code, but here, it is quite a bit easier. Before you start though, look at the scene graph. You'll see it's well organized through the use of containers, making things easily sorted and accessible.

Let's stick with that principle and create a new container to store the door animation. Collapse containers to see better, and then right-click the main scene graph entry and create a new container. Name it Tools. With a right-click, make that container active. Anything you add to the scene now will be part of that container. Go to the Assets library under Tools, Animators. Here, you can choose between our Rotation and Translation tools. Since we're dealing with pivot instead of sliding doors, we'll use rotators.

Here you will find the rotator tool that you need as well as a few samples. Simply drag the rotator tool and place it in front of the doors in the scene. Reposition it to where the hinges of the door should be. If you accidentally click somewhere else, the rotator disappears from the view. To select it again, you need to do so in the scene graph. To make the door react to the rotator, you need to make it a child of the tool. Select the door in the viewport.

Normally, you'd need to drag it from one container to the next in the scene graph, but that's sometimes difficult if there are too many objects listed. What I find to be a good alternative is to use Cut and Paste. So with the door selected, press Ctrl-X to cut it to memory, and then press Ctrl-V to paste it back again. Visually, nothing happens in the viewport, but in the scene graph, the door has now moved to the active container. All that's left to do is hierarchically link it to the rotator with a click and drag.

The effect is immediate and continuous. Select the rotator helper in the scene graph. There are different animation modes to choose from. You can also control speed and delay. To make the rotator react to the camera position, set the animation mode to Once, and then activate the Trigger option.

You can adjust the trigger distance or zone, set it to about 400cm or 4m, adjust the angle for the door opening, set it to a positive or negative value to set the door to open to the inside or to the outside. As an exercise, do the same for the other door.
Let's look at another tool that Twinmotion has to offer. Section Cubes. These are found under Tools, Sections. Drag the Section Cube into the scene.

Move it around to see the effect. As the name implies, the Section Cube cuts through the geometry to create cross-sections in your project. You can use Transform Tools to reshape the cube. You can also invert the operation if you so choose. You can change the highlight color.

Go ahead and hide the section box before moving on. Another tool you may find interesting is the Notes tool. You can add visual notes to the screen which you can potentially use as part of your design review. The process is very simple, yet again. From the Assets library, go to Tools, Notes, and drag a note into the scene into a particular spot, let's say the cafe's entrance. You can control its size, rotate it around, or you may opt to having it always facing the camera.

To control the space between the text box and its node, you can select the child object in the scene graph and move it around. You can change the color, or alignment, and of course write down a given note. In my case, I'm shamelessly paraphrasing a famous movie quote.

Experiment by placing a few more notes in the scene. Just make sure you hide them before moving on. Another simple but effective tool is the Measure tool. You'll find it under Tools, Measure. It's pretty self-explanatory, so we'll only be spending a passing moment on it using it inside the main building. Drag it into the scene and see how it snaps onto surfaces.

With it, you can easily measure the distance between surfaces, such as between two walls or between two floors. Constraints are on by default and you can make adjustments to the color, text position, and global scale.

The dimension text is made to follow the camera. If you're planning to use the same color for many different objects, consider storing the color so you can access it more easily. This is definitely more of a design review tool than a rendering tool but still quite effective. Before you move on, hide the Tools container. There's one more tool we need to mention, Reflection Probes. Reflection Probes are used to improve the quality of reflections in real-time environments.

However, it's worth noting that Reflection Probes are somewhat old technology and may not be so necessary as we move forward. Let's see how reflections are currently handled in the scene by looking at the façade of the main building. You can see the tree reflected in the glass panes but it's blurry and unconvincing. What's worse is that if you start moving closer to the façade, there comes a point where that reflection disappears. This coincides with the moment where the tree is outside the bounds of the viewport.

Twinmotion uses a technique called Screen Space Reflection or SSR. This means that for reflection to take place, the reflected object must be seen in the viewport. As you can see, it's not an optimal solution in AEC, although you can get away with it in games environments. Instead, you can use Reflection Probes to remedy that. You'll find them in the Asset Library under Tools, Reflection Probes. Reflection Probes capture the environment around them and project it back onto nearby reflective surfaces.

There are two types available, Spheres and Boxes. Drag a sphere reflection probe close to the curtain wall. Currently it doesn't have much effect, we are still only seeing the screen space reflections. You need to adjust the area of influence of the sphere. Set it to about 8 meters or 800 centimeters. Now you can see an effect. It's not perfect yet, but it's getting there. The biggest difference with what we had a moment ago is the fact that if you zoom closer,

you can still see the reflection of the tree even though the tree is not visible in the viewport anymore. The quality of the reflections is adjustable. Reflection captures are essentially bitmaps. You can increase or decrease the quality in the Preferences dialog. This is done under Edit, Preferences, where you can edit probes for resolution both in the viewport and at render time. I have already set them to 1024, but the default is lower at 256. Try different values to test viewport reflection quality.

However, I did mention earlier that reflection probes are a bit obsolete by today's standards. This is because rendering engines have evolved quite a bit in the last few years. Delete the reflection probe to go back to the SSR display. In the Ambience panel, switch to Render mode. Note how this project is set in real-time and uses the standard Global Illumination method.

Switch from Standard to Lumen. Lumen is the newer rendering technology used in both Point Motion and Unreal Engine. For all intents and purposes, you should rely on it as your go-to rendering method. You can see the effect immediately. The reflections are high quality and very accurate. What's more, the rendering in general is far superior. This can be mostly seen inside the building. Note the effect of bouncing light and color bleed on the various surfaces.

Switching back and forth will give you a better appreciation of the differences between Lumen and the older standard method. There is a third option. You could use path tracing, which acts as a traditional renderer giving you the best quality rendering available. You can adjust the quality by using presets or by editing the rendering parameters. Keep in mind that you need a high-end graphics card for path tracing to work.

Let's look at adding artificial lights or man-made lights to accommodate night scenarios. For that, you need to open the file named To-Lighting that's been provided to you. Before you move on, create a new active container in the scene graph named Lights to keep things tidy. All the lights you create in this exercise will be part of that container. By default, when you start a project, the daytime lighting scenario is provided to you. To set your lighting at night, you first need to change the time of day.

This can be done in the Eye menu in the viewport or in the Ambience panel. Interestingly, if you go beyond a certain hour of the day, after the sun sets, some aspects of your scene react to that change. A good example is the headlights and taillights on animated vehicles. Change the time of day going from day to night to see the cars light up.

However, you do need to place a few active lights in and around the project, which appears rather dark at night. Let's see what's available. Go to the Assets library under Lights category. You'll see many entries, but most are samples of lights with an IES profile. Essentially, all of those are spotlights. There are really four options to choose from. An Omni or Point light that emanates in all directions.

You can control the intensity. Its attenuation or how far it spreads. The color temperature. And whether it casts shadows, among other options. A spotlight on the other hand is more directional. It opens up in a cone so that you can control the beam. But otherwise, has roughly the same parameters as an Omni light.

Try an IES light such as IES 03. You'll notice it effectively is a spotlight. It has the same options, except for an IES profile defined in the Lights miscellaneous section. That profile ensures the light spreads in a particular way, the way the manufacturer intended. Incidentally, if you need to select a light in the scene, you can do so in the scene graph.

If you wish to select it in the viewport, you may or may not see an icon associated with the light. If you do not see the icons, press G to display them. The G key acts as a toggle. You also have a linear light, or a neon light as it's called, where you can control intensity, length and color, but not attenuation. Finally, there's also an Area light, and as you define parameters such as length, width and attenuation, you get a light that emanates in a box-like pattern.

This can be used to help with global illumination in difficult spots. As a side note, night lighting is where Lumen shines, no pun intended. You can better appreciate the difference between Lumen and Standard modes in night scenes. In addition to their regular parameters, all light types can be set to activate only at nighttime.

Currently, if you switch back to Day mode, the lights are still active. But if you select one of them and go to the Miscellaneous section, you can enable the Dusk to Dawn option. You can do the same with every light you have placed in the scene. If you try it now, you'll notice that the lights only activate around 7.30 or 8pm.

In addition to standalone lights, there are some assets in the library that have embedded lights in them. For example, go to Objects -> City -> Street Lights and drag in a street lamp. I'll use this one called Streamlight. Note in the scene graph that this asset is made of both geometry and a spotlight that you can control and adjust to your liking. However, not all assets have associated lights.

For example, try this bollard named Galvanic. It's just a simple mesh at this time, but you can help change it a bit. Try adding a self-illuminated material to the white covers. If you're using Lumen, the emissive material helps a little bit with the lighting. You can also add a full-fledged omni light to help illuminate the area around the bollard.

You can then parent the light to the bollard and send the bollard to the user library. You now have your own assets ready and available. If you make instances of any light in the scene, you'll be able to change the parameters of one light to update all duplicates. Keep on experimenting by creating your own light fixtures.
Next, we'll discuss media output.

Once your project is ready, you can output media to disk and share images and videos with your audience. Open the file named 3-Media that's been provided to you. Start by setting the time of day to around 4.30pm. We'll change that again later if we need to. Also unhide the animated people and the grass using the Scene Graph.

Go to the Media panel in the dock. Here, you can define still images, videos, and panoramas to export. There are also two other options that we'll discuss in a moment. To define a still image, the process is easy. Adjust the view to a shot you like, make sure Image Mode is active, and click the plus sign. This creates a snapshot that you can now edit independently from the editor. You can rename the view, but more importantly, you can adjust it in terms of time of day, exposure, weather, all of which would be parameters affecting this image and this image alone.

A simple example would be to have a shot in daytime and duplicate the image to get a shot at nighttime. You can now switch back and forth between the two. Another example may be to view the scene in a different season, by duplicating an image and changing the appropriate parameters.
If you change your point of view, you will need to use the Refresh icon to update the image. For some shots, you may decide to use a depth of field camera effect.

Other interesting applications may lead you to use special filters for certain images. At any time, you can quit Media Mode to go back to regular editing. Another type of media that you can use is a 360-degree panorama.

Much like with still images, you position your camera where you need it to be, I'll use the Caffe, and then go to the Media Panorama panel and use the plus sign. You get the same options you usually get with images, including camera effects and filters. The 360 panorama will be created once you save it to disk, which we'll do in a moment. Next up are videos. Go to that panel. First, position your camera where the video will start. We'll animate the view to go around the building.

The current camera position will be recorded as the first frame when you click the plus sign. Note that the video length is set by default to 10 seconds. We'll expand that to 30 to give ourselves enough time around the building. To animate the camera, move your view to another point, and then click the plus sign on the right side of the clip to create a new keyframe. Keep on moving. Move and adjust the camera position and create additional keyframes as needed.
At the end, duplicate the last keyframe to just let the camera settle in its position. Ultimately, each sub-clip can be set to its own time of day to animate that effect if you so choose.

Scrub the animation to see the results. Go back to the main video menu and rename the clip and then exit media mode. Now that you have defined your media, it is time to output it to disk. This is done by using the Export panel on the dock.

Here you can choose which media to export. For example, under Images, you'll find the still images you have defined. You can choose the ones you want to render. You can do the same with Panoramas and with videos. There are some restrictions when using the community version of Twinmotion. Images and videos are saved to HD format and will have a watermark on them.

Panoramas can be rendered as high as 6K in resolution. That's a small sacrifice to pay for free software. When you are ready to proceed, click the Start Export button. Choose or create an output folder and let the system process the data. This may take a while, especially when processing videos, so you may want to take a little break. Once the process is over, then you can view your files or share them with friends and clients.

Another way of sharing media is through Presenter. In the Media panel, choose Presentation. Here you can create a presentation that includes some or all of the media you've already defined. You can simply drag media and organize it on a timeline and you can mix between types. I think I'll use images and videos only for this and leave the panorama out. Once you have defined your presentation, you can go again to the Export panel.

You can blank out the previous outputs since they're already saved and include the presentation file you have just defined. If you export it, again be aware that it might take a while to render, but also... it will create a self-executable that allows others to interact with your project without having Twinmotion installed. Because of that fact, Presenter saves more than just media.

It compiles everything it needs to run the self-executable and therefore, presentation files tend to be large on the hard drives. The end result would look like this. And know that you can totally walk around and interact with your scene. Just select any image that you like and start walking around.
This leaves one additional media option to learn about, working with phases, coming up in the next and last video.

Phasing is a way to simulate a construction schedule. You organize phases on a timeline calendar and then hide or unhide components as needed for each phase. Open the file named For Phasing that's been provided to you. Go to the Media Phasing Group panel. Note that there's already a media file defined. We'll look at it, although you'll be creating your own in a second. Click the Phasing 1 thumbnail to open the timeline for it.

If you want, you can click the Zoom Out tool to view the extents of the phases, 9 phases that take about a year of construction work. If you scrub through the timeline, you can see the work evolving, from the main excavations all the way to fully constructed and inhabited projects. Exit Media mode. Let's look at how we can set this up. First thing you need to do is to define phasing content in the scene graph and scene graph containers.

Here it's already been done for you. Hide all the phase containers to effectively hide your project. Unhide them one at a time to see their content, and you'll have an idea how they were sorted. Go to the Phasing panel and create a new phasing calendar.

With the clip selected, make sure the container named Phase 1 is displayed in the scene graph and all other phase containers hidden. This represents the start of the work, the excavation work. Click Create Phase again to add a second clip. Unhide Phases 2 and 3 and hide Phase 1. Excavation is done and we have the foundations in place. Click Create Phase again to add a third clip.

This time, hide Phase 2, the workers and their equipment, and unhide Phase 4 as the walls start coming up. If you make a mistake, you can select the clip on the timeline and review what needs to be visible or hidden. Keep on going but make sure you select the last clip on the timeline before proceeding. Add other clips and adjust the visibility of containers accordingly.

At any time, you can scrub through the timeline to check your work. This is easy enough, but how do you output an animation of this phasing work? This is done by going to the Media video panel. Earlier, we used the video tool to keyframe camera motion but here, we just set it up to read the phasing calendar we defined.

Create a new video and set it to about 30 seconds in length as before. Go back one step and rename the video Mic Phasing but more importantly, expand the Details sub-panel and set the Phasing group to the new phasing definition you just created. That's it. From this point on, you simply need to output that video to disk as you have already learned.
This marks the end of this class. I hope you have enjoyed it.

Today, we looked at some of Twinmotion's additional features to complement the basics. You learned about tools that give you more flexibility when dealing with animation and general productivity. You learned about lighting and experimented with man-made lights to support night scenes. From there, you learned about media output and how to set up still images, panoramas and videos to export to disk. You also learned to export self-executable presentations that you can share with your clients and audience.

With that, others can enjoy your work without needing to have Twinmotion installed. Finally, you learned to work in Phases, which is capturing an animation of the phases of construction of your project. I hope you have learned something useful that you can apply to your work.

Hello everyone, and welcome to this session on Twinmotion to Unreal Engine. My name is Amer Yassine and I will be your guide today. The purpose of this class is to show you how to export your Twinmotion project to Unreal Engine for further processing. We'll cover the recommended workflows, as well as tips and tricks to ensure the best compatibility between the two apps. You'll first learn about setting the stage, and what plugins you need to help with the transfer.

You'll then learn to ingest the Twinmotion data into Unreal Engine in a couple of different ways, before you learn to manage lights, levels of detail and collisions. Finally, you will learn how to fix or replace those effects that didn't transfer properly. We'll be using Twinmotion Community Edition 2023.2 and Unreal Engine 5.3 for this class. And so, if you're ready, let's start!

The first step is to have a Twinmotion project ready. Use the TM2UE Twinmotion file that's been provided to you. You also need an Unreal Engine project on the receiving end. But before you create one, you will need to install a dedicated Twinmotion plugin. Use the Epic Games Launcher to access Marketplace. Look up the plugin named Datasmith Twinmotion Content for Unreal Engine.

Install it to Unreal Engine. In my case, I've already installed it to the 5.3 version. Next, start UE5 and create a new project using the blank architectural template and name it TM2UE5. First order of business is to ensure the plugin is enabled. Go to the plugin's dialog and search for Twinmotion.

Enable the Datasmith Twinmotion Content plugin you just installed and restart the project. Once that's done, close the plugin's dialog and create a new default level. Set the Sun and Sky to a more reasonable intensity of 100 lux. Adjust the post-process volume's exposure to a more constant setting.

Delete the camera and the floor. You won't need them for this project. Finally, move all remaining actors into a Lighting folder for better scene management. Save your level. Things are now ready on the UE5 end.

Back in Twinmotion. Again, make sure the provided TM2UE file is open. Consider the scene graph. The project has been neatly organized using containers. That's good news because although you could export the whole project in one sweep, sometimes it pays off to break it into parts for easier management. For example, you could hide all containers except Open Theater to export the hero building on its own.

The export process in itself is simple enough with the Datasmith Export feature accessible in the File menu. For this project, you will need four distinct exports to cater separately for the hero building, the context building surrounding it, vegetation and other props including characters and vehicles. These Datasmith files have already been extracted and provided to you so you won't need to waste time on that process.

I will mention this though, setting the time of day prior to exporting may make a difference. For example, animated cars at night display headlights and taillight effects that are based on decals. These will not export if the time of day is set in daytime. Next, we import these Datasmith into Unreal Engine.

Back in UE5, use the Quickly Add to the Project button on the main toolbar, and import the Datasmith file named Context.udatasmith that's been provided to you. You are asked for a location on disk, create a folder named Theatron. When asked for import options, make sure all options are enabled and import the file. You may get a warning or two. In this case, the warning is about a Twinmotion material using the Grunge feature, which is not compatible with UE5.

Aside from that, everything seems to be properly in place. Note the presence of multiple Twinmotion cameras that were derived from the Media panel in Twinmotion. Keep in mind that Datasmith doesn't cater for collision data, and LODs behave erratically at times. We'll look how to deal with that later in this class. Let's bring in another part of the project.

Repeat the import process, this time for the vegetation part. When you get to the Import Options dialog, disable cameras as you don't want them duplicated. Once the Datasmith file is imported, look at the Outliner. You have the Context and Vegetation folders representing the two Datasmith file hierarchies. Both contain a Background entry.

That's a duplicated actor representing the circular city background around the scene. You can safely delete one of those. The other thing you'll notice as you zoom in with the imported trees, is that although they import properly, there is a problem with the display. This promises to be fixed soon, but for now, the easiest fix is to save your level and all its assets, and restart the project.

The trees look better now, although that last LOD level leaves a lot to be desired. And as mentioned, Datasmith doesn't carry over any collision information between apps. Dealing with LODs and collisions one tree type at a time would be too time consuming. So let's look at an alternative way of importing the data. To delete all vegetation in the scene and in the project, start by selecting the Vegetation top parent in the Outliner.

Press Ctrl-Shift-D to select the hierarchy underneath and then press Delete. Confirm all deletion and then select the files and folders in the Vegetation folder in the Content Browser and do the same. Now that all vegetation is removed from the project, we'll import it again using a different technique. In the empty Vegetation folder in the Content Browser, right-click and create a Dataprep asset. Name it Vegetation.

Double-click the asset to edit it in the Dataprep Editor. Here, you can decide how to sort and adjust your incoming data in a node-based editor. Start by selecting the file to import, in this case the Vegetation Datasmith file. Click the Import button to see the file contents. Note that the Datasmith file contains duplicates of elements you already have in the scene, such as the background and the cameras.

To get rid of those, you can filter the selection using an actor label. You can type the name of an actor you wish to select, such as Background, and then add a Delete Objects node to that action. Add another actor label to the graph, this time looking for cameras. To select the child actors, add a Select Hierarchy node to the action.

And finally, a Delete Objects node to finish off that process. To test your work, click the Execute button on the toolbar. After a moment, you'll notice that the background and the camera actors have disappeared from the outliner. Next, consider that all the trees in the incoming file have the label Growth in them. Add a new actor label node based on the name Growth, and then add a Set LOD node to the action.

Disable Auto-Screen Size if you plan to define how the LODs will transition. Add three LOD array elements, or three LOD levels if you will. That should be enough for our purposes. Adjust the numbers, you can follow my lead or experiment with other numbers. This will take care of adding LODs for all trees. Similarly, add a Set Convex Collision to the action. Leave the default values as they are.

This will apply collision detection for all trees in the scene. Execute the recipe to test the results. This will take a while, but it's still faster than doing the work manually. Once you're happy, click the Commit button to send the results to the editor. Once you're back in the editor, save your data using the Save All button.

You still need to restart your project to refresh the texturing, but otherwise, you should be good to go. As good as visual data prep is, sometimes it may just be overkill. For the hero building, a simple import will work just fine. Import the theory.datasmith file as you have learned earlier. Again, make sure the Cameras option is disabled to prevent duplicates.

You'd still need to delete the duplicated background that is also part of this datasmith file. For the most part, everything seems to be working well, but there are adjustments to be made at the lighting level. All incoming lights are currently set to Static, as evidenced by the red warning in the viewport. It suggests that light baking is needed for the scene. If you're planning to use Lumen instead, all incoming lights should be set to Movable.

Other light issues can be viewed at night. Set the time of day to about 9pm. Some spotlights could use a burst of energy, but the bigger problem lies in the street lights and bollards. The lights associated with those should have shadow casting turned off to see any effects.

To fix all these issues, you need a tool to bulk edit lights. You can use the Light Mixer tool in the Window menu. The tool lists all the lights in your scene. It can also list properties that you need to edit. You can add or remove properties by right-clicking the menu bar. You already have the Mobility property displayed. Add Cast Shadows, Intensity, and Indirect Lighting intensity to the mix.

Select any of the entries in the Light Mixer and then press Ctrl-A to select all the lights. You can now easily change their mobility status to Immovable. The Light Baking Red warning doesn't disappear from the viewport, which needs a refresh. We'll do that in a moment. Scroll down the list and select Street Lights in the Light Mixer. Right-click and choose Select Immediate Children. Do it again on the sub-selection to ensure the whole hierarchy is selected.

Disable Cast Shadows to ensure they're off on street lamps and bollards. Unfortunately, the effect is not immediate in the viewport. Save your level and reload it to see the effect. Note also that the Light Baking message has disappeared. The Street Lights intensities could use a little boost.

In the Light Mixer, select all Streamlined entries and set the light intensities to 800 all around. Again, it is unfortunate that you must save and reload the level to see the effects. Here's hoping that this becomes more interactive in a future release. Go back to a time of day around 1pm when you're done. Next, we'll discuss LODs and collisions.

In general, the transfer of data between Twinmotion and Unreal is rather straightforward, but in some cases, you may encounter some glitches that require your attention. This is the case with the planters on the roof. Their LOD settings are quite aggressive. You'll also note that these planters are supposed to be identical and yet are using different static meshes for reference. Select the first planter using the Boxum static mesh reference.

Open that reference in the static mesh editor by double-clicking its thumbnail. Check the four existing LODs. Only the first two make sense. This is a low poly model we can do with just two LODs. Set the number of LODs to 2 and apply the changes.
Save the updates and exit the static mesh editor. Select all the planters and assign them to use the Boxum static mesh we just updated. Now they look better, even from afar.

Similarly, you can make quick adjustments to collisions. As mentioned, collisions are not carried over using Datasmith Interop. You can test this by going into play mode and see that you can walk through walls. Fortunately with architectural scenes, walls are often made of simple geometry and usually have a low poly count. This means that you can in fact use their geometry to detect collisions.

To do it in bulk, you can filter all wall objects in the Outliner and press Enter to select them. You can then right-click any of them and then use Browse to Asset. The associated assets are now selected in the Content Browser. Right-click on one of them and then choose Asset Actions, Edit Selection in Property Matrix.

A dialog appears in the search box type Collision and then change the Collision Complexity to Use Complex Collision as Simple. For practice, do the same with the Curtain Panels actors to be able to collide with the curtain walls.

Remember this method is only effective with simple geometry. With complex geometry, you would want to assign simple collision shells. Of course, your motion is now restricted inside the main building. In Twinmotion, the doors are made to open when you get close to them, but this effect has not made the transition to Unreal Engine. In the next step, you replace the doors using a blueprint.

As you can see, not all data makes the jump correctly from Twinmotion to Unreal. Another example of this is in the form of the animated doors. They are animated in Twinmotion as you get close to them, but that functionality has disappeared with the transfer to UE5. The rotators are still in place acting as hinges, as are the hierarchies, but not the animation. The good news is that you can replicate the effect in UE5 with the help of a simple blueprint.

Adjust your view outside the doors on the upper floor. Also set Play Mode to activate from the current camera location. In the Theater folder in the Content Browser, create a BP for Blueprint subfolder. In it, create a new actor blueprint and name it DoorOpen. Double-click the blueprint to edit it.

Select one of the doors and browse to the asset in the Content Browser. Add a new Static Mesh component to the blueprint. Because the door asset is selected in the Content Browser, it will be automatically added to the Blueprint viewport. Simplify the name of the Static Mesh component in the blueprint as Door.

Select the default scene root entry and add Child Actor. This will act as a non-renderable null object and will be used as a hinge for the door. In fact, name it Hinge. Adjust the position of the door so that its right side is aligned with the hinge at 0,0,0. Use a Snap value of 1cm for better control. Parent the door to the hinge.

Next, you need a trigger box. Select the default scene root again and add a Box Collision component. Name it Trigger. Adjust its position and Extents to match the door. And also make sure it extends enough in the Y direction to allow a fair distance to trigger it as you step in.

In the Event Graph tab, delete all existing nodes, you won't need them. Select the Trigger component and go lower in the Details panel. Click the On Component Begin Overlap and On Component End Overlap events. This will add nodes where you can define what happens when you step in or out of the trigger volume.

Drag the Hinge component into the working area, and add Set Relative Rotation to it with a 90 degree Z rotation angle. Connect the action to the Begin Overlap event. This will set the door to rotate 90 degrees when you step into the volume. Compile and save, and then drag an instance of the blueprint to the scene to test the results.

Test the scene in Play mode. At this stage, the door opens with a snap and remains open. You could expand on the blueprint by duplicating nodes and resetting the rotation angle to 0 as you end the overlap. To duplicate nodes, select them and then press Ctrl-D.
Compile and save. The effect works but the snapping is bothersome. You need a smoother rotation. To create a smoother rotation, add a Timeline node.

Rewire the connections to the door on Begin Overlap, and double-click the Timeline node to edit it. Add a float track named Door Opening. Here we'll define an animation curve to smoothly open the door between two angle values. With a right-click, add two keyframes to the curve. Select them both and set them to Auto Tangents.

This will add ease-in, ease-out effects to the door opening and closing. Set the first key at a time position of 0 with a value of 0. This means that the door is closed before you get into the trigger volume. Set the second key to a time position of 2, as in 2 seconds, and a value of 110. This essentially means that it'll take 2 seconds for the door to rotate 110 degrees. Use the Zoom buttons on the toolbar to view the extents of the curve.

Go back to the event graph when done and note the new door opening pin representing the new timeline curve. Right-click the new rotation track in the Set Relative Rotation event and split the structure pin. This separates the Vector3 XYZ rotation and separate float tracks. Wire the door opening curve to the Z Relative Rotation of the hinge. To reverse the action of the door, you only need to wire the On Component End overlap node to the reverse pin of the timeline.
You can delete any excess nodes at this time. Compile and save the blueprint, then test your work. The door should be behaving much better now.

Delete the test instance when done. Next, you will replace the Twinmotion doors with the blueprint. Start with the upper door on the right as viewed from the bridge. It is actually made of two actors, a mesh door and a non-renderable rotator. You won't need the door at all as the blueprint you have defined already contains a duplicate, so go ahead and delete it. Select the remaining rotator actor. Make sure the blueprint is also selected in the Content Browser.

Right-click the selected actor in the Outliner and replace it with the blueprint. Test your work. Note that the door is swinging to the incorrect side. Arguably the easiest way to fix this is by setting its Y scale to minus 1. This will reverse the swing.
Repeat the procedure with the left door. This one will swing correctly and does not require Y scale adjustments. Repeat the procedure for the doors at the ground level.

These will require slight adjustments to their X scale as well, as they are a little wider. A value of 1.35 should work well. You can now use the doors to get in and out of the building. Save your work before moving on.

In this last video, you add the final touches to the scene by importing the missing elements. These include people, cars, and some additional props. Import the last Datasmith file, the one named Props, as you have learned before. There will be some issues with the import that you can check in the message log. These mostly relate to animated people and animated cars that do not translate well between Twinmotion and Unreal Engine.

Delete the redundant background and get closer to the scene. Note that any posed characters imported correctly, but that any animated characters did not. That's the import restriction as it currently stands. Anything else that is static, like furniture and decorations, imported flawlessly. Interestingly, all vehicles did import, but they are static. Their animations didn't come through.

Again, this is a known restriction that we currently have. However, note the green squares in front and behind each car. These are decal objects for the headlights and taillights. Unfortunately, their material did not translate correctly between Twinmotion and Unreal Engine, so we'll need to fix that. Create a new folder under Content Theatron, Props, Materials, and name it Decals.

Create a new material named MCarLights. Set the new material to be used as a deferred decal and set the blend mode to Translucent. Look in the Textures folder and note the two imported textures TLightMaskFrontBC and TLightMaskRearBC. These represent the front and taillights on the cars.

Drag the TLightMaskFrontBC texture into the newly created material. Convert the node to a parameter and call it Light Mask. This will allow you to change it at the instance level. You could wire it directly to the emissive channel, but let's give ourselves a bit more control. Press 3 and click in the material editor to add a color node. Again, make it a parameter and name it Tint.

You'll use this to tint the mask which will be useful for the taillights. Make the default color white though. Press M and click to add a Multiply node. Multiply the two nodes and then add another Multiply node before you wire that to the emissive channel. The second Multiply node will be useful to control the intensity of the effect. Add a Scalar node, S on the keyboard, and name it Intensity.

Wire it to the second Multiply node and set its default value to 1. Save the material and close the material editor. Create two material instances named miHeadlights and miTaillights. Adjust their parameters such as intensities and colors. You may need to revisit these values again.

Also make sure the taillights are based on the appropriate mask image. Use the Outline Research Box to filter all the Decal F actors in the scene. Note that the Twinmotion material assignment didn't carry through. Assign the miHeadlights material you just created. And repeat the procedure for the taillights or Decal R.

Switch to Nighttime to view the effects. Lastly, you can help the night scene by adding a bit of a moon effect. Add a Directional Light to the scene. It will conflict with the SunSky system. Rename the actor Moonlight and move it to the Lighting folder.

Note the error in the viewport. You need to adjust the Forward Shading Priority value. Search for it in the Details panel and set it to 1 to remove the conflict. Look also for Atmosphere and set the Sunlight Index to 1. This will bring the sky and clouds into effect. Change the light color to a blue that you like and reduce the intensity.

This will make the environment a bit more visible at night instead of being drowned in darkness. It will not affect the scene much in daytime. Save your project now that you have transferred your Twinmotion scene into UE5. This brings us to the end of this class. I hope you have found it useful.

So there's a ton of different ways to generate these points. And then after that, what we do is we have a number of different tests that you can set up.
